title: Ruth Boaz Grain Account
subject: Contracts
stem:
BARMATRIX Q# 14378 — Christian variation: 14378_ruth_boaz_grain_account

Boaz, a grain farmer, and Ruth, who operates a flour mill, have dealt with each other in hundreds of separate grain contracts over the last five years. In performing each contract, Boaz delivered the grain to Ruth and, upon delivery, Ruth signed an invoice that showed an agreed-upon price for that delivery. Each invoice was silent in regard to any discount from the price for prompt payment. The custom of the grain trade is to allow a 2% discount from the invoice price for payment within 10 days of delivery. In all of their prior transactions and without objection from Boaz, Ruth took 15 days to pay and deducted 5% from the invoice price. Boaz and Ruth recently entered into a contract for a single delivery of wheat at a price of $300,000. The same delivery procedure and invoice were used for this contract as had been used previously. Boaz delivered the wheat and Ruth then signed the invoice. On the third day after delivery, Ruth received the following note from Boaz: "Payment in full in accordance with signed invoice is due immediately. No discounts permitted. s/Boaz."

Which of the following statements concerning these facts is most accurate?
call: Which of the following statements concerning these facts is most accurate?

choices.A: The custom of the trade controls, and Ruth is entitled to take a 2% discount if she pays within 10 days.
choices.B: The parties' course of dealing controls, and Ruth is entitled to take a 5% discount if she pays within 15 days.
choices.C: Boaz's retraction of his prior waiver controls, and Ruth is entitled to no discount.
choices.D: The written contract controls, and Ruth is entitled to no discount because of the parol evidence rule.

rightExplanation: B is correct. Gold Key: Under the UCC, when sources of meaning conflict, the ranking is fixed: express terms beat course of performance, which beats course of dealing, which beats usage of trade — the parties' own repeated practice outranks general industry custom. The invoice here is silent on discounts, so there is no express term to beat. The parties' course of dealing — hundreds of contracts in which Ruth paid in 15 days, deducted 5%, and Boaz never objected — supplements the silent writing and outranks the grain trade's 2%/10-day custom. Silver Key: when two answers each cite a real past-practice source, name the axis — whose practice: these parties' own, or the industry's? The deciding fact is "in all of their prior transactions and without objection." Ruth may deduct 5% if she pays within 15 days. Boaz's third-day note changes nothing: it is a unilateral attempt to strip a term that is already part of the agreement's meaning.

wrongExplanations.A: A cites a real rule — usage of trade can supplement a silent writing — but runs the hierarchy backwards. Gold Key: course of dealing, when inconsistent with usage of trade, controls. These parties' own practice (5%/15 days across hundreds of contracts, never objected to) is more specific than the grain trade's general 2%/10-day custom, so the course of dealing displaces the custom. A would be the answer only if the parties had no relevant history of their own.
wrongExplanations.C: C presupposes a waiver, and the facts contain none. A waiver requires an existing contractual right that one party excused — but every invoice was silent on discounts, so there was never an express no-discount right for Boaz to waive and later retract. The 5%/15-day practice is not an indulgence Boaz granted; it is part of what the agreement means. Silver Key: before crediting a "retraction of waiver" answer, point to the term that was supposedly waived — if the writing is silent, the waiver frame has nothing to attach to, and the question is one of interpretation, not waiver.
wrongExplanations.D: D misstates how the parol evidence rule works under the UCC. UCC § 2-202 — the UCC's embodiment of the rule — bars contradiction of a final writing by prior agreements, but it expressly allows the writing to be explained or supplemented by course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade, even without any ambiguity. Gold Key: the UCC parol evidence rule never blocks course-of-dealing or trade-usage evidence; those sources are always available to fill in a silent writing. And the writing here is silent on discounts — D cannot derive a "no discount" term from words the invoice does not contain.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text:
- C is cut on a fact relation visible in the stem. "Retraction of his prior waiver" requires something that was waived — an existing right Boaz excused. But every invoice was silent on discounts, so the stem contains no no-discount term for Boaz to have waived. The choice assumes a fact not in evidence.
- D is partially wounded at CUT — the stem says the invoice is silent on discounts, yet D claims "the written contract controls" the discount question, asking a silent writing to speak. The full kill (the parol evidence rule affirmatively admits course-of-dealing evidence) needs the Gold Key, so D is anchor-assisted, not structurally false.
- A and B both survive: each states a real interpretive source supported by stem facts.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: A vs. B fight on a single axis: when the writing is silent, which past-practice source supplies the term — the industry's general custom or these parties' own repeated practice? The splitting fact is "in all of their prior transactions and without objection from Boaz" — hundreds of contracts of party-specific conduct.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: The axis does not resolve from the stem alone; it takes the taught hierarchy anchor. Gold Key: course of dealing prevails over usage of trade. The parties' own 5%/15-day practice displaces the grain trade's 2%/10-day custom. Residual answer: B.

studentScript: The invoice is silent on discounts. C invents a waiver — nothing in the facts was ever waived. D asks the silent writing to speak, and the UCC parol evidence rule lets past practice supplement a writing anyway. That leaves A versus B: the industry's custom or these parties' own practice. Gold Key: course of dealing beats trade usage. Hundreds of their own contracts at 5%/15 days without objection. Pick B.

A.signal: A and B both point to real past practice in the stem; A picks the industry's practice, B picks these parties' own. The stem's loudest history fact — hundreds of their own contracts without objection — sits on B's side.
A.lawyer: UCC § 1-303(e)(2): course of dealing prevails over usage of trade when they are inconsistent. Trade custom would control only absent a party-specific course of dealing.

B.signal: The only choice grounded in the stem's most specific, most repeated fact: all prior transactions, 5%, 15 days, no objection.
B.lawyer: UCC § 2-202(a) allows a final writing to be explained or supplemented by course of dealing; § 1-303(e) ranks that course of dealing above the inconsistent trade usage. The agreement includes the 5%/15-day term.

C.signal: A 'retraction of a waiver' needs something that was waived. The invoices were always silent on discounts — the stem never shows a no-discount right that Boaz excused. The doctrine has no fact to attach to.
C.lawyer: Waiver is not in play: the 5%/15-day practice defines the agreement's meaning rather than excusing breach of an express term. Boaz's unilateral third-day note is also not a modification — UCC § 2-209 modification requires agreement of the parties.

D.signal: The stem says the invoice is silent on discounts, yet D claims the written contract resolves the discount question — it asks a silent writing to speak. The full defect needs the Gold Key.
D.lawyer: UCC § 2-202 expressly permits a final writing to be explained or supplemented by course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade; the parol evidence rule bars contradiction, not supplementation, and silence cannot be contradicted. Columbia Nitrogen and Nanakuli apply the principle broadly.

goldKeys.statement: Under the UCC, sources of meaning rank by specificity: express terms beat course of performance, which beats course of dealing, which beats usage of trade — the parties' own repeated practice outranks general industry custom.
goldKeys.trigger: a party-specific payment practice conflicts with an industry custom under a silent writing
goldKeys.unlocks: B over A — the parties' 5%/15-day course of dealing displaces the 2%/10-day trade custom.

goldKeys.statement: The UCC parol evidence rule (§ 2-202) bars contradicting a final writing, but it never blocks course of performance, course of dealing, or usage of trade — those may always explain or supplement the writing, even without ambiguity.
goldKeys.trigger: an answer invokes the parol evidence rule to exclude past-practice evidence against a silent writing
goldKeys.unlocks: the D trap — 'the written contract controls because of the parol evidence rule.'
goldKeys.authority: UCC § 2-202(a); Columbia Nitrogen Corp. v. Royster Co., 451 F.2d 3 (4th Cir. 1971); Nanakuli Paving & Rock Co. v. Shell Oil Co., 664 F.2d 772 (9th Cir. 1981)

silverKeys.statement: Split this array in half first: C and D deny any discount and must explain where a no-discount term comes from in a silent writing; A and B grant a discount and fight over whose practice counts. The silence kills the first pair's footing before you ever rank the second.
silverKeys.trigger: four choices that each crown a different source of contract meaning

silverKeys.statement: When two surviving answers each cite real past practice, name the axis: whose practice — these parties' own, or the industry's? Then find the stem fact that personalizes it ('in all of their prior transactions and without objection').
silverKeys.trigger: one answer says 'custom of the trade,' another says 'the parties' course of dealing'

remediation.title: Silent writing: rank the practices
remediation.signal: A signed writing is silent on a term; both an industry custom and the parties' own repeated practice speak to it.
remediation.studentMove: Split the array (discount vs no-discount), cut the choices that need the silent writing to speak, then ask whose practice is more specific.
remediation.tinyRule: Parties' own course of dealing beats general trade custom; the parol evidence rule blocks contradiction, never supplementation.
remediation.trap: Picking the trade custom because it sounds official, or crediting the seller's after-the-fact 'no discounts' note as a retracted waiver.
